content_voiceover: Two engineering strategies are used to extend the half-life of clotting factor products, and boards love to test the mechanism. PEGylation is chemical coupling of polyethylene glycol to the protein, which increases its hydrodynamic volume so the kidney can no longer filter and clear it as quickly. The second strategy is fusion proteins, where the Fc fragment of an immunoglobulin G or albumin is genetically fused to the recombinant factor. This works because Fc and albumin are natural substrates of the neonatal Fc receptor, FcRn, on endothelial cells, which recycles them back into circulation instead of routing them to lysosomal degradation. That FcRn recycling pathway is the same mechanism that extends the half-life of IgG antibodies physiologically, so the fusion proteins essentially hijack an existing salvage pathway.
keypoints: PEGylation: PEG conjugation increases hydrodynamic size, reduces renal clearance
Fusion proteins: Fc-IgG or albumin fusion exploits FcRn recycling
FcRn receptor on endothelium rescues Fc/albumin from lysosomal degradation
Both strategies extend plasma half-life of factor VIII/IX products
keypoint_voiceover: Two half-life extension strategies: PEGylation, which enlarges the molecule to dodge renal clearance, and Fc or albumin fusion, which exploits the FcRn receptor's recycling pathway on endothelial cells to rescue the protein from lysosomal breakdown.
